name: whosthere
desc: LAN discovery tool with a modern TUI written in Go
why: LAN discovery TUI that surfaces ARP and mDNS chatter, a readable door into local network protocols.

brief.what_it_is: Whosthere is a Local Area Network discovery tool written in Go, with an interactive terminal UI. It runs mDNS and SSDP scanners concurrently, sweeps the local subnet with TCP/UDP connection attempts so the OS fills the ARP cache, then reads that cache to list devices. Each device is enriched with a manufacturer name from OUI lookups. It can run as the TUI, as a one-shot CLI scan that prints results (optionally JSON), or as a background daemon with a small HTTP API. Devices can be given aliases, stored in a local bbolt database.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a friendly way to answer the question every network administrator asks: "Who's there on my network?" It says it was created primarily for educational purposes and home network exploration.
brief.how_it_works: The mDNS and SSDP scanners listen for multicast service announcements. For ARP, the sweeper opens TCP/UDP connections to each address in the subnet, which triggers ARP resolution by the OS without elevated privileges, and then reads the ARP cache to find live hosts. Optional port scanning checks a configurable list of TCP ports on found devices.

brief.install_notes: Other install routes in the README: nix profile install nixpkgs#whosthere on NixOS, yay -S whosthere-bin on Arch Linux, or pre-built binaries from the GitHub releases page. Building from source needs git and make, with a Go toolchain implied. No elevated privileges are needed. Config is optional: YAML at --config, WHOSTHERE_CONFIG, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/whosthere/config.yaml, or ~/.config/whosthere/config.yaml. Every key can also be set with WHOSTHERE__-prefixed environment variables. For clipboard copy (y/Y keys), install pbcopy (macOS, built in), clip.exe (Windows), or xsel/xclip (X11) or wl-copy (Wayland) on Linux and BSD.
brief.standout: It gets device discovery without root by making the OS populate the ARP cache through ordinary TCP/UDP connection attempts, then reading that cache, rather than sending raw ARP packets. It combines that with mDNS and SSDP in one terminal UI with regex search, theme switching, and a daemon HTTP API.
brief.status: unknown. The README has a release badge and a releases page, but it shows no release date, last commit date, or maintenance note, and I did not fetch the GitHub release or commit pages.
brief.caveats: Listed platforms are Linux, macOS and Windows. Clipboard features depend on external copy tools being installed. The port scanner should only be used on devices you have permission to scan. Scanning subnets larger than /16 sends a large amount of traffic, and the config file warns about this. If two interfaces share a subnet with all_interfaces enabled, devices can be merged because they are keyed by IP. Importing a changed aliases file overwrites aliases for every MAC in it. The README says results may not be comprehensive and that it is not a professional monitoring tool. Licence type was not visible in the README, only a badge.

entry.title: whosthere
entry.tldr: A terminal UI that lists every device on your LAN by combining mDNS, SSDP and the ARP cache, with no root needed.
entry.deeper_look:
Whosthere is a LAN discovery tool written in Go. Run it and a terminal interface fills with the devices on your local network: phones, TVs, printers, laptops, whatever answers. Each one is tagged with a manufacturer name looked up from its MAC address prefix (the OUI). You can give devices aliases, search with regex, and switch themes.

Under the hood it runs three kinds of discovery at once. The mDNS and SSDP scanners listen for multicast announcements, the chatter devices make to advertise themselves. For the ARP part, it opens ordinary TCP and UDP connections to every address in the subnet. That makes the operating system resolve each address with ARP, and whosthere then reads the OS ARP cache to see which hosts are alive. In the README's words: "This technique populates the ARP cache without requiring elevated privileges."

That trick is the door into something larger. Tools like this normally send raw packets and need root. Here you can watch the same protocols from the outside: which devices announce themselves, which only show up in the ARP table, and what your home network says when nobody is asking. The README says it was made mainly for education and home network exploration.

Beyond the TUI there is a one-shot scan that prints results (optionally as JSON), and a daemon mode with a small HTTP API. Optional port scanning checks a configurable list of TCP ports on the devices it finds.
entry.install:
brew install whosthere
# alternatives: go install github.com/ramonvermeulen/whosthere@latest, or pre-built binaries from the GitHub releases page
# no elevated privileges needed; clipboard copy needs pbcopy, clip.exe, xsel/xclip or wl-copy

try_this.what_happens: Opens the interactive TUI and starts discovering devices on your local network.
Runs a single five-second scan and prints the devices it found.
Does the same scan and saves the results as pretty-printed JSON.

entry.whats_unique: It finds devices without root by letting the OS fill its ARP cache through ordinary connections, then reading the cache instead of sending raw ARP packets. It puts that together with mDNS and SSDP in a single TUI.
entry.caveats: The README says results may not be comprehensive and it is not a professional monitoring tool; only scan devices you have permission to scan, and the maintenance status is unclear from the README.
